entries.value: The accounts aren’t mine. They used my daughter’s name. But I was there to get the tube, yes.

If the tube went to the lab, I was finished, my daughter was finished. I knew what was in that horse’s blood. I told Owen, ‘Give it here’; he wouldn’t. The shoe mallet was in my hand. I tied the horse at the back so it would look like a kick. The instructions came from above; ‘it mustn’t win,’ they said, and I made sure.
At home. The horses are fed at ten; I leave at nine. Owen went into that stall, the horse got spooked. It happens.
He narrows his eyes and looks at the stable door.

· Cause of death: skull fracture; a single blow to the left temple.
· The shape of the wound matches a horseshoe mark, but its angle matches not a horse’s kick but the swing of a tool held by a standing person.
· No horsehair or dung in the wound; there is iron rust.
· Time of death: 22.00–23.30.

Against Southern Liaison over the last four days:

· 412 accounts, $1.9 million in total.
· 300 of the accounts were opened from the same three phones; one in the name of Grant Ainsley’s daughter.
· In the event of a win, payouts were to go to a sub-account of Pacific Liaison Trust.
The steward takes his own sample of the horse’s blood; the trainer is beside him.
The strapper finds the steward in the stall, the horse tied up.
A shout in the stable, ‘the tube goes to the lab tomorrow’; then a float door.
Where did the steward’s missing sample tube go?
Under the straw in the trainer’s float
I sleep in that stable, sir.

I sleep in the room above the stall. Around eleven I heard voices, someone shouted, ‘the tube goes to the lab tomorrow’. Then a float door. In the morning I found the steward. The horse was tied up; I didn’t tie it, that horse is never tied at night.
He laces his fingers together and squeezes.
What happened in the stable last night?
There was no tube in the forge.
The tube never reached the laboratory.
It was recorded that the tube was hidden in the float.
The death was ruled an accident; the horse ran in the cup and lost.
Grant Ainsley was arrested; Southern Liaison was withdrawn from the cup. Pacific Liaison Trust’s sub-account was frozen.
Declan Rafferty was questioned; the real hand went free.
Sione Taufa was arrested; the mallet stayed in the float.
There is no horsehair in the wound, the angle matches a human swing; the horse was tied at the back.

The shoe mallet and the steward’s missing tube came out of his float; one of the accounts the bets piled into is in his daughter’s name. The syndicate promised him a bonus for ‘following instructions’.
The owner gave the instructions, but he wasn’t in the stable that night and the mallet isn’t his.
All the farrier’s hammers are in place; someone else had taken the old shoes.

Grant Ainsley’s horse float (stable car park):

· In the toolbox, a short-handled mallet with an old horseshoe riveted to its head; dried blood and rust on the shoe.
· Under the straw, a sealed sample tube; on its label the steward’s initials and ‘S. Liaison’.
· The float door’s hinge freshly oiled.
My job is the horses’ health.
Harriet Combe flew to London on the midday flight. Her new employer declined an interview.

I looked at the horse’s hind shoes; no blood, no hair. And this horse is calm. Last night the steward asked for the horse’s blood; I didn’t take the sample, he took it himself. The trainer was beside him, very tense. Tomorrow I fly to London; a job offer.
She folds her arms across her chest and looks at the stable door.
Could the horse have kicked him?
I ride the horse I’m put on.
As I was told. Nobody said ‘don’t let it finish in the first four’; they said ‘don’t push it’. There’s a difference. Mai Pham rang me last week; there were loads of bets against the horse.
He fixes his eyes on the ground.
How were you going to ride the horse in the cup?
Betting line opened: accounts, stakes, connections.
Ownership line opened: syndicate agreements, trust connections.
Stable line opened: floats, toolboxes, stable comings and goings.
Risk analyst at the betting company.
If the numbers say something, I listen.
Against a favourite, four days out, small stakes but from hundreds of accounts. I was the one who told Steward Pryce. He said, ‘I’ll look at the horse’s blood.’
She pushes her glasses up her nose.
What kind of movement did you see?
He fell and hit his head

A racing steward lies dead in the stall of the cup favourite; the first report says ‘horse kick’.
49, trainer at Flemington; trains the horse ‘Southern Liaison’.
31, risk analyst at a betting company.
A syndicate. I’m the representative. The money comes from a trust; asking its name is none of your business. They named the horse.
He straightens his tie without loosening it.

On the morning of 1 November 2030, at the Flemington stables, racing stewards’ inspector Owen Pryce (44) was found dead in the stall of the horse ‘Southern Liaison’. He had a severe head wound; the initial assessment was ‘horse kick’.

The strapper Deng Akol found the body at 05.10. The trainer Grant Ainsley, the owner Declan Rafferty, the jockey Shane Keogh, the veterinarian Harriet Combe and the farrier Sione Taufa were at the stable in the morning. Mai Pham of a betting company had called earlier to report ‘unusual movement’.
Request permission to search the trainer’s float
Request an examination of the stall
I nail the shoes on, I don’t know the rest.
My hammers are by the forge, mate; all six in place. I keep the old shoes, anyone who wants one takes one; last week Grant took two, ‘for luck’, he said.
He fiddles with a nail in his apron pocket.
The mark in the wound apparently looks like a horseshoe.

Southern Liaison’s stall:

· Blood only on the door side; the horse was tied at the back of the stall, its rope taut.
· Drag marks in the straw, from the door inwards.
· The steward’s sample bag in the corner; one of twelve slots empty, seal broken.

The vet had to be heard before the autopsy; after that she was gone. Two of the three lines were open at once: the stable line gave the mallet, the betting line the daughter’s name, the ownership line the bonus.
The horse hadn’t kicked. It was only standing there.

The favourite owned by Pacific Liaison Trust was not to win the cup. The trainer Grant Ainsley drugged the horse; hundreds of accounts bet against it. The steward Owen Pryce took a sample of the horse’s blood. At night Ainsley demanded the tube back, didn’t get it, struck him with the horseshoe mallet and tied the horse at the back to fake a kick.

The ‘Southern Liaison’ syndicate:

· Sole partner: Pacific Liaison Trust (Melbourne). Representative Declan Rafferty.
· A ‘results bonus’ for the trainer Grant Ainsley: ten per cent if the horse wins, thirty per cent ‘if the syndicate’s instructions are followed’.
· Instructions are given verbally.
A short-handled mallet with an old horseshoe riveted to its head; it came out of the toolbox in the trainer’s horse float.
The steward’s sample bag; one of twelve slots empty, seal broken.
A transcript of the bets piled against the horse four days before the cup.
